theme: 3 terms on closures: passing code around in Swift

terms.definition: A block of code you can store in a constant and pass to a function to run later.
terms.example: Pass a closure to the button, and it runs when the user taps.
terms.code:
let greet = { (name: String) in
    print("Hi, \(name)")
}
greet("Mina")

terms.definition: A closure written after the closing parenthesis of a function call, instead of inside it.
terms.example: Use a trailing closure here, and the sort reads much cleaner.

terms.definition: A list in square brackets at the start of a closure that copies values when the closure is created.
terms.example: Add a capture list, so the closure keeps the old value.
terms.code:
var count = 1
let show = { [count] in
    print(count)
}
count = 2
show()

quizzes.question: In this code, what is the block written after the call, outside the parentheses, called?
Which term is a block of code you can store in a constant and pass around?
In this code, what is `[count]` called, the part that keeps the value 1?
quizzes.code:

video.title: Closure, Trailing Closure & Capture List in 2 minutes | iOS Daily English Day 6
video.description:
Learn to talk about closures in Swift: Closure, Trailing Closure and Capture List, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
Closure - A block of code you can store in a constant and pass to a function to run later.
Trailing Closure - A closure written after the closing parenthesis of a function call, instead of inside it.
Capture List - A list in square brackets at the start of a closure that copies values when the closure is created.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Morning, Jake. Why is the badge number wrong?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I change `count` after a tap, but the screen shows the old number.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Do you use a closure for the tap?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. A closure is a block of code I run later.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. You can pass a closure to another function.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: For sorting, I wrote the closure inside the parentheses.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It works, but a trailing closure is cleaner.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What is a trailing closure?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You write the closure after the parentheses, not inside them.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice. So `sorted { $0 < $1 }` is a trailing closure.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now the bug. Do you have a capture list in that closure?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, `[count]`. I copied it from another file.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A capture list copies the value when you create the closure.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it keeps 1 and ignores 2. I thought it was a compiler bug!

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ha, no. Remove the capture list, and the closure reads the latest `count`.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Fixed. It shows 2 now.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great. Keep a capture list only for old values.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Got it. I learned a lot today. Thanks, Mina!
